posts.author: pearlv
posts.content_md:
I want to be able to clear the pale brown pyrogallol stain from my holographic film after bleaching (RCA developer/EDTA bleach/AGFA combination). I am preswelling and multiple exposing reflection holograms and want to overlay my holograms over photographs. 

I remember hearing from someone somewhere that you can clear the stain using potassium permanganate so the film is completely transparent. Does anyone know about this - and whether using that chemistry would effect the image over time?

Thanks Pearl

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
I have this post from the original forum at holographyworld but don't know who posted it. I also have not tried it so...

> Many stains respond well to this:Stock Solution AWater at 60 to 80°C (140 to 176°F) ...350 mLPotassium Permanganate ...50 gthen Water at 20°C (68°F) ...600 mL(Dissolve the permanganate crystals completely in the hot water before adding the cooler water.)Stock Solution BWater at 20°C (68°F) ...900 mLSulfuric Acid (concentrated) ...100 mL________________________________________________________Soak film (plate) until an even purplish tone is evident.Then soak in the following to clear the purple:10% Sodium Bisulfite Clearing BathWater at 20°C (68°F) ...900 mLSodium Bisulfite ...100 gDissolve the sodium bisulfite crystals in the water. Store the solution in a tightly closed container. Both the 'Permanganate' and the 'Bisulfite' solutions keep well in closed containers. The 'Permanganate' can be corrupted by overt halogens and stuff left over from bad rinsing, or crud in the water or... and a scum will seem to form on the top of its container...sluff this off before dipping your Hologram in it. Also in cold weather, and with the introduction of certain elements, the 'Permanganate' will percipitate out of solution and looks like old rust floating on the bottom...dump it and make a new batch. If you let the fluid evaporate, the 'Permanganate' will harden into platlets at the bottom and is not too easy to clean up (sort of looks like brown rust layers). Anywise all this reaction and aging detail gives a headsup on what to look for to know its time to make up some anew.

And for clearing the permanganate stain an ascorbic acid solution is much more efficient...

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
This is a stain remover that has been successful for me. It is from a paper entitled "Reversal Bleaching for Low Flare Light in Holograms", R. L. Lamberts and C. N. Kurtz, Applied Optics Vol. 10, No.l 6 June 1971. It was also published in Kodak Pamphlet P-302 on how to process their Type 120/SO-173 Holographic Plates/Film. It seems to be the first paper on using a revesal bleach in holography, pre-dating van Renesse's *Pyrochrome* system. The authors were with the Kodak Research Laboratories.

They used pyrocatechol as the developing agent and were worried about the stain it would give. So they used Tray Cleaning chemistry to remove the stain.

The recipe:

KODAK STAIN REMOVER S-13

Solution A

Water 750 ml

Potassium Permanganate 2.5 g

Sulfuric Acid Conc. 8.0 ml

Water to make 1 L

Solution B

Water 750 ml

Sodium Bisulfite 10 g

Water to make 1L

No times of immersion or washing cycles were given, but they do say "The latter (S-13) remove brown stain that appear after development. These solutions also make the final plate much less subject to darkening from printout."

I have used these brews on Pyro'ed Agfa plates and it works fine. There is no rinse between the permanganate and bisulfite baths, but I would give a decent wash after that.

That Sodium Bisulfite is a nasty one, with a lung-scorching odor much worse than the dreaded PBQ!

Good luck!

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **Michael:** "clearing"?

Right. The permanganate badly stains the emulsion.

> **Ed Wesly:** You need to get rid of the permanganate. What are the details of the ascorbate bath?

An ascorbate solution (say, 50g ascorbic acid/L) clears the layer almost instantly. As that clearing solution actually re-activates the emulsion, thorough water rinsing is required.
